questions.skill: Restrict trigonometric functions to define inverses
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why is sin x not invertible on all real numbers?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is sin x not invertible on all real numbers?

choices.text: It repeats values (for example sin 0 = sin π = 0), so it is not one-to-one.
Its outputs are larger than 1 for large x, outside the range of an inverse.
It is not defined for negative x, so an inverse would be incomplete.
It is an odd function, and odd functions never have an inverse.

questions.correct_answer: It repeats values (for example sin 0 = sin π = 0), so it is not one-to-one.
questions.grading_note: A function must be one-to-one to have an inverse. The others are false: sin x stays between -1 and 1, is defined for negative x, and being odd does not prevent an inverse.

questions.skill: Restrict trigonometric functions to define inverses
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: What is the standard restricted domain of sin x, and why does it work?
questions.prompt_markup: What is the standard restricted domain of sin x, and why does it work?

choices.text: 0 ≤ x ≤ π: sin is increasing there and takes every value from -1 to 1 once.
-π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2: sin is decreasing there and takes every value from 0 to 1 once.
0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: sin takes every value from -1 to 1 there, which is all that is needed.
-π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2: sin is increasing there and takes every value from -1 to 1 once.

questions.correct_answer: -π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2: sin is increasing there and takes every value from -1 to 1 once.
questions.grading_note: On [-π/2, π/2] sin rises from -1 to 1.

questions.prompt: Why would 0 ≤ x ≤ π not work as a restricted domain for an inverse of sine?
questions.prompt_markup: Why would 0 ≤ x ≤ π not work as a restricted domain for an inverse of sine?

choices.text: sin is not defined at x = π, so the interval is not closed.
sin is negative everywhere on that interval, so it misses positive values.
sin increases then decreases there, so values repeat (sin(π/6) = sin(5π/6)).
sin is increasing on that whole interval, so it is one-to-one there.

questions.correct_answer: sin increases then decreases there, so values repeat (sin(π/6) = sin(5π/6)).
questions.grading_note: The function must be one-to-one on the restricted domain. The others are false: sin is defined at π, is nonnegative on [0, π], and is not increasing on the whole interval.
